https://www.dw.com/en/military-aircraft-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NnDH The plane involved in the crash is similar to the one in the picture (FILE: August 10, 2026) Image: Steven Mohr/SNS/picture alliance Advertisement A military aircraft carrying 25 passengers and seven crew members crashed in southern Nigeria , authorities said on Monday. Nigerian President Bola Tinubu later said all 32 people on the plane had died in the crash, extending his "deepest condolences" to the deceased's loved ones. The aircraft was on a routine mission to Lagos, Nigeria's economic hub, when it crashed in the Igbokoda area of Ondo state, Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo said in a statement. Wreckage located Keyamo said the aircraft disappeared from radar at around 9 a.m. local time (7:00 a.m. GMT) and was later found to have crashed about halfway through its journey from Edo state to Lagos. He said the wreckage had been located near a naval base. The Nigerian Air Force identified the aircraft as an ATR-42 and said an immediate search and rescue operation had been launched. A video circulating on social media showed a small crowd gathered near a river as rescuers searched the area by boat. Locals told AP news agency about what they had heard and seen. "The plane cleared some trees. We found some body parts, some clothes and shoes," one of the locals said. Edited by: Wesley Dockery Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://aa.com.tr/en/asia-pacific/moscow.text: Asia - Pacific Europe Moscow says Europe uses ‘Russian threat’ to justify higher defense spending ‘Irresponsible and shortsighted European political elite is playing a dangerous game,’ says Russian Embassy in Dublin Burak Bir 30 September 2026 • Update : 30 September 2026 LONDON Russia on Wednesday accused European countries of using an alleged Russian threat to justify higher defense spending and rejected claims that Moscow plans to invade Europe. In a statement, the Russian Embassy in Dublin rejected claims that Russia plans to launch a military invasion of Europe or escalate an alleged hybrid campaign against European countries. “The slogan of ‘Russian threat’ is being recycled in the Western media on a daily basis,” the embassy said in a statement shared on US social media platform X. It claimed European countries were seeking to justify higher defense spending and the “overall militarization of Europe,” as well as further financial, military and political assistance to Ukraine. The embassy said there was nothing to support claims of an “imminent Russian invasion.” “Moscow’s position on the security situation in Europe has always been consistent and confirmed yet again by President (Vladimir) Putin on September 25 – we have no plans, no reasons and, most importantly, no real motives for aggravating situation with Europe,” it said. Referring to Gallant Boar 2026, a joint military exercise by Lithuania, Poland and France, the embassy claimed the exercise was “specifically aimed” at Russia’s Kaliningrad region on the Baltic Sea. “There has been information that NATO is preparing air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and Kaliningrad region,” it said. The Kaliningrad region is a Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea between Poland and Lithuania and separated from mainland Russia by Lithuanian territory. Calling the issue a “matter of grave concern” to Russia, the embassy said: “The irresponsible and shortsighted European political elite is playing a dangerous game.” ‘Moscow would be ready to use all its arsenal’ The embassy cited Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov as saying recently: “If the West attacks us, we will respond and it would be completely different war and a very brief one.” Speaking at the International Youth Festival in Yekaterinburg on Sept. 16, Lavrov said that if Europe attacks Russia, the resulting war would be “completely different” and “very brief.” The embassy said Moscow would be ready to use its entire arsenal, “including nuclear weapons,” to defend its territory if NATO countries tried to isolate the Kaliningrad region from the rest of Russia. “Under such scenario, the risk of armed confrontation is high with the likelihood of Russia using preemptive strikes against centers of decision-making in the Alliance countries already at the early stage of the conflict,” it warned. “It is a matter of utmost seriousness and should be treated by Europe as such,” the embassy added. On Tuesday, the Russian Embassy in the UK also warned that any attempt by the UK or NATO to blockade the Kaliningrad region would be met with a response using all means, including nuclear weapons. news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription contact_the_ombudsman is_there_an_error_in_this_story LATEST NEWS All 5 arrested in probe into suspected $1.1 million fraud involving NATO vessels UK pledges additional missile support to Ukraine after Burnham-Zelenskyy meeting Berlin urges Israel to lift working ban on German journalist 8 US states sue OpenAI, citing risks ChatGPT poses to children US watchdog sues over Trump's son-in-law Kushner serving as presidential envoy Ebola outbreak in DR Congo expands to new health zone: WHO Algeria’s death penalty provisions take effect for forest arson, child kidnapping See All Belgium orders NASAMS air defense system for $1B 'Strong indication' of Iran's involvement in suspected plot near RAF base: UK premier

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwkg.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations By Vicky Wong Published 24 October 2026, 12:17 BST Updated 3 hours ago Ukraine now has a "stable connection" to Starlink, its defence minister has said, after its military suffered days of restricted connectivity on the satellite internet network. Kyiv relies on the Starlink and its military-grade counterpart Starshield for piloting drones and operations within Ukraine, but last week accused US President Donald Trump of telling owner Elon Musk to place limits on it. This meant drones would lose connection when travelling at 161km/h (100mph) or more, it said. Trump denied doing so before saying Musk had "put it back". Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said that speeds of more than 400km/h were now possible on the network, indicating that full capability had been restored. "This result is above all important for our front, for our soldiers, for the operation of drones, for logistics and for communications," he said in a statement on Saturday. Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield. Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, which Musk said was controlled by the US military when he suggested the Pentagon could be behind the recent issues. Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work. The debacle over Starlink began last week, and emerged during a broader diplomatic row between Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure. Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies. Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher. While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war . Zelensky said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied. Meanwhile, fighting on the ground continues. Russia's ministry of defence wrote on Telegram on Saturday that their air defences shot down 616 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones, striking a number of regions across the country, including Russian-annexed Crimea. Sergey Aksyonov, the region's Moscow-backed governor, said restrictions on electricity and water had been put in place because of power cuts caused by the drone strike. Meanwhile, Ukrainian authorities said they struck a missile component manufacturer, a chemical plant and an aircraft at a military airfield inside Russia in the past 24 hours. They also said that Russia carried out 88 air strikes using 309 glide bombs and 10,270 kamikaze drones on Friday. Figure caption, Watch: Who controls Ukraine's access to Starlink?
